specPoints.text: understand that the feasibility of a reaction depends on: i the balance between ∆ S system and ∆ S surroundings , so that even endothermic reactions can occur spontaneously at room temperature ii temperature, as higher temperatures decrease the magnitude of ∆ S surroundings so its contribution to ∆ S total is less Students should be able to calculate the temperature at which a reaction is feasible . Students may also use ∆ G = ∆ H - T∆ S system in answers, although this approach is not a requirement of the specification.
understand and distinguish between the concepts of thermodynamic stability and kinetic stability

primer.text: A reaction is feasible when the system and surroundings entropy changes combine to a positive total. Gibbs free energy packs the same test into one expression, delta G = delta H - T delta S. This note sorts feasible and infeasible sign combinations, finds the temperature where feasibility flips, and separates thermodynamic permission from kinetic reluctance.

lessons.title: When the total entropy says yes
lessons.opening: A reaction is feasible when system and surroundings entropy changes add to a positive total. Three sign patterns pass the test: both positive; surroundings positive and bigger than a negative system; system positive and bigger than a negative surroundings term. The state ladder - solid below liquid below gas - predicts the system's sign at a glance.
keyPoints: For delta S total to be positive and the reaction feasible, three sign patterns work: both terms positive; surroundings positive outweighing a negative system; system positive outweighing a negative surroundings.
Entropy generally increases along solid, liquid, gas, so state changes in the equation hint at the system's sign.
Magnesium burning to MgO turns a solid and a gas into a solid, so the system's entropy falls, but the strongly exothermic surroundings term wins and the reaction is spontaneous.
Ethanoic acid with ammonium carbonate is endothermic, yet a gas produced from a solid and a liquid makes the system term win, so the reaction runs.

low.restatement: Add the two entropy books: any sum above zero is feasible; the state ladder predicts the system's sign and the enthalpy sign predicts the surroundings'.
low.analogy: Two bank accounts deciding a purchase: either balance can carry the day if the other is not too far in debt.
low.examPointer: Read the state symbols first - losing a gas usually means the system term is negative, so the surroundings must pay.

medium.restatement: Feasibility is a sum, not a veto: each term can be negative provided its partner is positive enough; the state ladder and the enthalpy sign set the two terms' directions.
medium.analogy: A seesaw with two riders: whichever side carries more weight tips the verdict.
medium.examPointer: Quote a sign pattern ('surroundings positive and larger') rather than just 'spontaneous'.

lessons.title: Gibbs free energy: the one-line test
lessons.opening: Gibbs free energy packs the entropy sum into one expression: delta G = delta H - T delta S. Feasibility demands delta G at or below zero. Mind the units - delta S must be divided by 1000 to match delta H's kilojoules.
keyPoints: The Gibbs equation is delta G = delta H reaction - T delta S system.
Delta G is quoted in kJ mol^-1, with T in kelvin and delta S system converted from J K^-1 mol^-1 by dividing by 1000.
A reaction is feasible when delta G is equal to or less than zero.
The Gibbs route is equivalent to the total-entropy route, gathering both drivers into one number.

low.restatement: Delta G = delta H - T delta S; feasible means zero or negative; convert delta S to kJ K^-1 mol^-1 before substituting.
low.analogy: A till receipt: the enthalpy price minus a temperature-scaled refund (the entropy term) leaves the final bill.
low.examPointer: The /1000 conversion is the most common lost mark - write it explicitly.

medium.restatement: Temperature sits multiplying the entropy term, which is exactly how heating can flip a verdict: the refund grows with T until the bill turns negative.
medium.analogy: A deposit refunded more generously every year you wait: eventually the refund covers the price.
medium.examPointer: Delta G = 0 is the turning point - quote it when asked for the flip temperature.

lessons.title: Exothermic reactions and temperature
lessons.opening: For exothermic reactions delta H is negative, so the verdict hinges on the entropy sign. A positive system entropy makes both terms negative: feasible at every temperature. A negative system entropy fights back as T rises, and above a flip temperature the change stops being feasible - though the small size of entropy changes makes that rare in practice.
keyPoints: In exothermic reactions delta H is negative.
If delta S system is positive, both terms are negative and delta G is negative at any temperature, so the reaction is always feasible.
If delta S system is negative, the T delta S term is positive and grows with T, so at very high temperatures delta G turns positive and the reaction is not feasible.
Because entropy changes are much smaller than enthalpy changes, exothermic reactions are usually spontaneous at normal conditions.

low.restatement: Exothermic plus positive delta S: always feasible. Exothermic plus negative delta S: feasible until high T flips it.
low.analogy: A shop discount always applied (negative delta H): a further bonus (positive delta S) keeps it attractive, while a hidden fee that grows with time (negative delta S) eventually kills the deal.
low.examPointer: The 'always feasible' case is the exam's favourite single-line answer.

medium.restatement: Temperature scales only the entropy term, so exothermic changes resist flipping: the enthalpy anchor is large, and T must be extreme for the entropy term to overpower it.
medium.analogy: A heavy boat with a small sail: normal winds cannot turn it, but a hurricane might.
medium.examPointer: Expect feasibility-at-temperature questions: compute delta G at the given T and compare with zero.

lessons.title: Endothermic reactions and temperature
lessons.opening: Endothermic reactions start with a positive delta H, so their fate depends entirely on the entropy sign. A negative system entropy dooms them at every temperature; a positive one needs heat, becoming feasible only once T delta S outweighs delta H - the story of blast-furnace extraction working hot but failing cold.
keyPoints: In endothermic reactions delta H is positive.
If delta S system is negative, both terms are positive, delta G is positive, and the reaction is never feasible.
If delta S system is positive, the term -T delta S is negative and grows with temperature, so the reaction becomes feasible at high temperatures.
Metal extraction in the blast furnace illustrates the pattern: unsuccessful at low temperatures, working at around 1500 degrees C for iron.

low.restatement: Endothermic plus negative delta S: never feasible. Endothermic plus positive delta S: feasible only above the flip temperature.
low.analogy: A gym membership that always costs money (positive delta H) plus a reward (positive delta S) that scales with attendance: keep attending and it eventually pays.
low.examPointer: The blast furnace is the stock example - quote roughly 1500 degrees C for iron.

medium.restatement: Heat is the lever for endothermic changes: heating boosts the T delta S term until it covers the enthalpy price, which is why many extractions wait for furnace conditions.
medium.analogy: Sweating an asset: hold it long enough at the right temperature and the returns finally cover the cost.
medium.examPointer: The 'never feasible' case pairs two unfavourable signs - the fastest exam verdict.

lessons.title: The temperature of the flip
sourceHeadings: Summary of factors affecting Gibbs free energy
lessons.opening: The flip temperature is where delta G crosses zero, so T = delta H / delta S once both are on the same scale. The aluminium oxide plus carbon example converts a positive enthalpy and positive entropy into one threshold: 1336 kJ mol^-1 over 0.581 kJ K^-1 mol^-1 gives about 2299 K.
keyPoints: The summary diagram gathers the four delta H and delta S sign cases and their temperature verdicts.
Delta G becomes negative when T delta S exceeds delta H, so the flip temperature solves T = delta H / delta S.
For aluminium oxide with carbon, delta H = +1336 kJ mol^-1 and delta S = +581 J K^-1 mol^-1, so T = 1336/0.581 = 2299 K.
The conversion of delta S from J to kJ is the essential step before dividing.

low.analogy: A thermostat point: below it the room stays cold (infeasible), above it the heating wins (feasible).

lessons.title: Thermodynamic versus kinetic stability
lessons.opening: Permission is not speed. Thermodynamic stability asks whether delta G is negative; kinetic stability asks how high the activation energy sits. Methane sits quietly in oxygen for thermodynamic reasons yet never burns unlit; hydrogen peroxide decomposes spontaneously on paper but waits for a catalyst such as manganese dioxide.
keyPoints: Thermodynamic stability asks whether a reaction is feasible under the stated conditions, with delta G negative.
Reactions are more likely to be feasible when delta H is negative or delta S is positive.
Kinetic stability refers to speed: a high activation energy makes a reaction kinetically stable even when feasible.
Methane is thermodynamically primed to burn but kinetically stable until ignited; hydrogen peroxide decomposes feasibly at 298 K yet needs an MnO2 catalyst in practice.
A catalyst offers an alternative route with a lower activation energy without touching the thermodynamics.

low.restatement: Feasible (delta G negative) is permission; a high Ea is reluctance. Catalysts lower Ea, never delta G.
low.analogy: A door left unlocked (feasible) at the top of a cliff (high Ea): reaching it is another matter; a lift (catalyst) changes the climb, not the lock.
low.examPointer: Pair the words: thermodynamic = whether, kinetic = how fast.

medium.restatement: The Gibbs verdict and the activation barrier are independent ledgers; a reaction may pass one and fail the other, which is why fuels wait for sparks and peroxides wait for catalysts.
medium.analogy: A raffle you have already won (thermodynamics) whose prize sits behind a maze (kinetics): winning and collecting are different tasks.
medium.examPointer: Answer 'why doesn't it react?' questions with Ea, never with delta G.

glossary.definition: Whether a reaction is thermodynamically allowed, tested by delta S total or delta G.
The quantity delta G = delta H - T delta S whose sign is the feasibility verdict.
Reluctance to react caused by a high activation energy, regardless of feasibility.

workedExample.prompt: Aluminium oxide reacting with carbon will not proceed at room temperature. Given delta H = +1336 kJ mol^-1 and delta S = +581 J K^-1 mol^-1, calculate the temperature at which the reaction first becomes feasible.
steps: Both delta H and delta S are positive, so delta G turns negative once T delta S exceeds delta H.
Set delta G = 0, which gives T = delta H / delta S.
Convert delta S to kJ K^-1 mol^-1: 581 J K^-1 mol^-1 = 0.581 kJ K^-1 mol^-1.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The reaction becomes feasible at about 2299 K.
